newsitem.title: FRANCE: Airbus posts 1996 sales of $8.8 billion.
newsitem.headline: Airbus posts 1996 sales of $8.8 billion.

text.p: European aircraft maker Airbus Industrie said on Monday it had turnover last year of $8.8 billion, down from $9.6 billion in 1995, based on deliveries of 126 aircraft last year.

Although Airbus delivered more units last year than the 124 planes in 1995, the lower sales figure in 1996 was due to fewer deliveries of the higher value wide-body aircraft, a spokesman for the aircraft grouping said.
Airbus is a consortium of France's Aerospatiale, Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG, British Aerospace and Spain's CASA.

The four partners reached a preliminary accord last Friday to restructure the Airbus consortium into a limited liability company to meet the challenge set by the planned merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas of the United States.
Airbus said in a statement its net increase in orders for 1996 stood at 301 planes, based on 326 firm orders from 31 customers valued at $23.6 billion, and 25 cancellations of previous orders.
But once memoranda of understanding and letters of intent are taken into account, Airbus had 1996 commitments for 498 planes, worth $34.4 billion, excluding options.
It has previously only announced firm orders based on signed sales contracts and deposits received but said it had adopted its competitors' practice of announcing the total number of commitments.

That looser definition allowed Airbus, locked in a dogfight with archrival Boeing to secure a half share of the world market, to say it had a 42 percent share for 1996 sales of aircraft seating more than 100 passengers.

In the 125-350 seater product segment where Airbus competes directly with Boeing, Airbus said it had a 57 percent market share in 1996. Airbus does not field a competitor to Boeing's 777 giant twinjet or the 777 jumbo, which give the U.S. firm a monopoly in the large capacity area.

Airbus said it expected its 1998 production rate to rise further to 220 planes. "Continued predicted strong growth will also see a further increase in total production during 1998 to some 200 aircraft," it said in a statement on its 1996 sales.
The company also announced a 45 percent increase in the 1997 production rate to total deliveries of 183 aircraft and that it expected its 1998 rate to rise further to 220 planes.
That planned output increase meant Airbus would be turning out around 14 narrow-bodies a month in 1997 and 18 in 1998, compared to the average seven per month last year.

The Airbus partners have made major productivity gains which has meant Airbus has also cut the lead time between orders and deliveries to some nine months for a narrow-body in the A320 product family from between 12-14 months two years ago, the Airbus spokesman said.
For wide bodies in the A330/340 range, the gap has narrowed to 12-14 months from 18 months, he said.
